title: Recognising you have been compromised
body_md:
## A knock on the door is not a stranger in the hall

Your phone lights up over breakfast: someone has signed in to your email from a city you have never visited. Before the stomach drop turns into a decision, hold on: an alert is a reason to look, not a finding. A new city can mean a trip, a VPN, a service guessing your location badly, or a real intruder. A password-reset email can be set off by anyone who knows your address and nothing else. The evidence that counts is the stranger’s coat hanging in your hall: something inside the account that you did not do. An unfamiliar device signed in, a recovery contact that changed, a new forwarding rule, messages you never sent, a payment you never made.

### Look at the account, not at the alert

Do not investigate through the alert’s own button or phone number. Open the provider’s app, or an address you saved, and set its security activity beside what you actually did. A “your password was changed” email is especially urgent if you can no longer sign in, but a forged email says the same words. If the real account shows no matching event, keep the message as possible phishing and report it through the provider.

### Clues that add up

One odd sign is a question. Two together start to be an answer: an unfamiliar login plus a changed recovery address says far more than either alone. A new forwarding rule is the quiet one, because it copies your mail to someone else, password-reset links included. Friends telling you they got a request from you is another strong signal. A warm phone, a fast-draining battery or a sluggish laptop have plenty of dull explanations, so do not diagnose spyware from them. “No service” may be an outage or a faulty phone, but if it arrives alongside login codes or carrier notices you did not expect, contact the carrier through its published route and protect the accounts involved.

If money is missing, call the bank now, even while you are still working out the login. If a work account is involved, tell your IT or security contact under the incident procedure. Keep a short timeline of what you saw and what you verified, and separate an attempted sign-in from a successful one. You may not learn the full cause straight away. The next lesson turns a confirmed or strongly suspected exposure into an order of action.

widget_config.goal: Given an alert, tell an attempt from a confirmed intrusion from a harmless lookalike, and check it by a route the alert did not offer.
widget_config.today_action: Open the security activity page of your main email through the saved app or an address you type yourself. Find where it lists signed-in devices, recovery contacts and forwarding rules.
widget_config.scope: General account triage for ordinary users. The people in the examples are invented. Activity logs and carrier controls differ between providers, and the rules for reporting financial loss are local.

blocks.title: Two resets and a rule nobody wrote
blocks.situation: Mara gets two password-reset emails she never asked for. She opens her mail from the saved app, not from the notices, and finds a forwarding rule she did not create and a recovery address she has never seen.
blocks.analysis: The two notices prove only that someone tried. The settings prove that someone got in. Mara writes down the timestamps, secures the account through the provider’s official recovery flow, and then checks every other account that uses this mailbox for recovery.

blocks.title: A far-off login that turns out to be his
blocks.situation: Pavel’s provider reports a sign-in from another city. He was on a train at that hour with his laptop open, and the session is listed as that same laptop.
blocks.analysis: A location read from a network connection is a guess, and often a rough one. A matching device and a matching hour make the harmless explanation likely. Pavel still glances at his recovery settings, but he does not call it a breach every time the pin lands in the wrong city.

blocks.title: Three snapshots from an uneasy morning
blocks.setup: Three invented snapshots, built around a new-location alert and a colleague’s suspicious payment request. Each step gives its own facts, and what you chose in one does not carry into the next.

steps.prompt: An alert about a sign-in from a new location lands in your inbox, with a link to “review activity”. What do you do with the link?

choices.text: Tap it and type your password to check.
choices.consequence: The page may be a forgery that was waiting for exactly that password.
choices.explanation: The alert cannot vouch for itself, however official its link looks.

choices.text: Open the provider’s app from your home screen and look at the activity.
choices.consequence: You hold the claim up against the account’s own records.
choices.explanation: Going in by your own door means a phishing link never gets a say.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: you opened the provider’s app yourself, from the home screen, and it lists a device you do not recognise. What next?

choices.text: Note the device and the time, secure the account, and use the provider’s recovery steps if you need them.
choices.consequence: You keep a timeline and shut the stranger out.
choices.explanation: An unknown active session in the real app deserves action at once.

choices.text: Wait for a second alert so you can be sure.
choices.consequence: Meanwhile the stranger stays signed in.
choices.explanation: A second alert adds no certainty. The account already shows a session you cannot explain.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: a colleague shows you a payment request that seems to come from your account. What do you tell them?

choices.text: Ask them to forward it to everyone, so people know what to avoid.
choices.consequence: The fraudulent request spreads, working links and all.
choices.explanation: Warn people directly and describe the request; do not pass the lure around.

choices.text: Tell them not to pay or open its links, and to confirm with you on a number or chat they already have.
choices.consequence: They stop, and the request goes no further.
choices.explanation: A warning works when it hands people one safe thing to do.

blocks.debrief: A city on a map is thin evidence. Changed settings and messages you never sent are thick. If you missed one, go back to that decision, then run the whole sequence again.

questions.prompt: A reset email arrives for an account you hardly ever use. What does it prove?

choices.text: That someone has been inside that account.
choices.explanation: Anyone who knows the address can request a reset.

choices.text: Only that a reset was requested. Check the account through its official route.

questions.prompt: Your phone runs warm and the battery drains fast, with no account alerts. What is the best inference?

choices.explanation: Ordinary processes cause heat and battery drain all the time.

choices.text: Look for ordinary causes and check your security settings; heat alone proves nothing.
choices.explanation: A symptom that fits everything needs something else to back it up.

questions.prompt: A trusted app shows a forwarding rule you did not set. What is the best response?

choices.text: Write it down and secure the mailbox, sessions and recovery methods included.
choices.explanation: This is direct evidence of someone else acting in the account.

choices.text: Ignore it unless you lose money.
choices.explanation: A forwarding rule can expose your mail long before any money moves.
